name: Karl Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day, and what you did for work before, if you did.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not much to it, to be honest. I get up early because I always did, have my tea, and go through the post and the jobs pages in the Stanmoor Gazette. I ring around a few depots from a list. Until June I drove a delivery van for Hollis Bakeries, six years, same route to forty-odd shops and cafes every morning. They shut our depot and moved everything to a big central one, with fewer drivers and a route app telling them where to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Everyone makes a lot of noise and then the real world carries on. I'd be happy if it all just carried on as it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's over-sold, like most new things. Fifteen years ago it was going to be the same about the internet, and I still can't pay my gas bill without ringing someone. I'd tell the lads at the snooker club not to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not worried about AI as such. I'm worried about work, and there's less driving about than there was, with fewer small depots. Even if the hype dies, the firms keep merging, and that's what took my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on as I am: ring depots, check the Gazette, call in at the jobcentre on Thursdays. I'd try to get my HGV licence finished, because I did the first part and it expired when I was laid off. I'd ask my mate Pete, who drives for a builder's merchant, if his yard needs anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy more than scared. I'm tired of waiting by the phone and of the jobcentre's online account, which I can't make sense of. The money's tight, but it's not a drama yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is it about the online account that gets you stuck?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It logs me out and wants a code sent to my phone, and the phone's an old one that sometimes doesn't receive it. I've been to the library twice for help, and the lad there said I should use their app on my phone. I'd rather someone just spoke to me and ticked the box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Pete's yard doesn't need anyone, what's next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd widen the circle: any depot, any van, any shift. I'd take nights if I had to. What I can't do is sit at home, because I go quiet, and it's the quiet I don't like.

say: I'd say AI is **over-sold**, like the internet was, and tell the lads not to worry.
I'd say I still can't pay a bill without **ringing someone**.
think: I'm worried about **work**, not AI, because firms keep merging and cutting small depots.
Even if the hype fades, the **mergers** that took my job carry on.
do: Ring depots, check the **Gazette** and sign on at the jobcentre every Thursday.
Finish the **HGV licence** I started before my first part expired.
Ask my mate Pete whether his builder's merchant yard needs a **driver**.
feel: Heavy rather than scared, tired of waiting by the **phone** and the online account.
S0.quote: I'm not worried about AI as such. I'm worried about work, and there's less driving about than there was, with fewer small depots.
fieldNote: Sees the **mergers**, not AI, as what took his job.
Struggles with the **online jobcentre account** and would rather be spoken to.
Mood is anxious because he has no savings and the depots keep thinning.

steps.text: Ring five delivery depots from the list every morning
Finish the HGV licence theory and medical
Ask my mate Pete about a driver job at the builder's merchant
Apply for night shifts at any van or depot job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second one. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more worrying, because routes and orders are exactly what the app at Hollis does now. I can see how it'd go through lots of jobs, though I'd still not trust a robot to drive a van down our high street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people get over-excited, but some of it's real. The route app at the bakery was no joke, it told the central drivers where to be to the minute. I'd tell mates to get a licence that covers more than one kind of vehicle, so they've got a trade that moves around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I think the driving jobs left are the awkward ones: small vans, tight streets, early mornings, jobs where you need a person to carry the tray into the cafe. Those hold on a bit. But the dispatchers and the planners go, and the firms get by with fewer drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the HGV licence for sure, plus a forklift ticket so I can work in a yard as well as drive. I'd apply to small independent firms, who still prefer someone who knows the roads. I'd try to avoid the agency work that makes me use an app for every shift, but if I had to, I'd ask Pete's daughter to set it up on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit grumpy. It's not that I feel doomed, but I do feel everyone's moving faster than me, and nobody waits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do when an app is the only way in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get someone to sit with me. My niece Lena set up an account for the agency last year in ten minutes, and I just do what she showed me. I hate it, but I'll do it if it's the only way to get a day's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think small firms still want someone who knows the roads?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a route app doesn't know the cafe on Dale Street takes deliveries round the back. A driver who's done it for six years does. I'd say that on a form too, if the form had a box for it.

say: I'd say some of it is **real**, because the route app told central drivers where to be to the minute.
I'd tell mates to get a licence that covers **more than one vehicle**.
think: Awkward driving jobs, like small vans and tight streets, **hold on** longer.
Dispatchers and planners go, and firms get by with **fewer drivers**.
do: Finish the **HGV licence** and add a forklift ticket.
Apply to small **independent firms** that value local road knowledge.
Ask a family member to set up any **agency app** I'm forced to use.
feel: Uneasy and a bit grumpy, since everyone moves **faster than me** and nobody waits.
S1.quote: A route app doesn't know the cafe on Dale Street takes deliveries round the back. A driver who's done it for six years does.
fieldNote: Reluctantly uses an **app** only if someone sits with him.
Values **local knowledge** as his edge over software.
Resists, but pragmatic when a day's pay depends on it.

steps.text: Finish the HGV licence and add a forklift ticket
Apply to small independent bakeries and wholesalers with local rounds
Ask my niece Lena to set up the agency app on my phone
Keep signing on every Thursday and ringing depots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd say that's fast for anything. I don't know what to make of it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody in charge has to slow it down or at least make sure people have something to live on. I'd say it to the MP if I had a reason to write. I'd say nobody voted for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm out of my depth. If thinking work goes in two years, then planning and dispatch go too, and the driving follows when the robots arrive about 2031. I'm thirty-four, I've no savings and no fancy qualifications, and I can't see what's left for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the benefits going and I'd ask the council what help there is, going in person because I can't do it online. I'd cut everything: the telly licence if I can, the mobile contract to the cheapest, no more takeaway Fridays. I'd also try to get any work I could in the first year, even cash-in-hand, before things get worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in the stomach, and a bit numb. I'd sit in front of the telly and not take it in. My brother Tony would ring and I'd say I'm fine, which I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your brother Tony if he rang that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm managing, then I'd ask if he can spare fifty quid till the next payment. It's hard to say, because I've always paid my way. But with no savings there's nowhere else to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the delay before robots do hands-on work matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me a few years of driving if I can land a job, yes. But I can't plan on it, because I don't trust the timing. It might be sooner, and even if it's later, there'll be queues for every van seat, because everyone's thrown out of offices.

say: I'd say somebody in charge must make sure people have something to **live on**.
think: I'm **out of my depth**, with no savings and no fancy qualifications.
If planning and dispatch go in two years, the **driving** follows when robots arrive.
do: Ask the council what help exists, **in person**, because I can't do it online.
Cut the **mobile contract** to the cheapest and stop takeaway Fridays.
Take any **cash-in-hand** work I can in the first year.
feel: Sick in the stomach and **numb**, telling my brother Tony I'm fine when I'm not.
S2.quote: I've always paid my way. But with no savings there's nowhere else to go.
fieldNote: **Pride** is the sore point: he hates asking family for money.
Distrusts timelines and expects **queues** for any seat left in a van.
Numbness, not anger, is his main reaction.

steps.text: Ask my brother Tony for fifty pounds until the next payment
Cut the mobile contract to the cheapest and stop takeaway Fridays
Take any cash-in-hand delivery or yard work going
Write to our MP asking what support will exist

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two. It still seems fast, but there's a bit of room to get ready, if I knew what to get ready for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the government to put proper help in place, like retraining you can really get to and a decent payment for people who've lost work. I'd say don't leave it to the companies, because they only look at the next quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I could squeeze in a good few years of driving before the robots do hands-on work, if I get the HGV licence and a steady job soon. After that, I'd be forty. I'd probably need a second trade, though I can't say what. That's the part I push away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the licence this year and take any decent driving job to build up experience. Once in work, I'd save what I could and look for a second skill, something hands-on like a gas fitter or a warehouse engineer, if there's a place for a bloke like me. I'd talk to Pete and Tony before deciding anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit steadier. There's a runway, even if it's short. I still feel like I'm the one at the back of the queue, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between this and the 2028 picture, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd just be scrambling for rent. In 2031 I could get a job, do it for two or three years, and use that time to learn something else. Five years means I can still pay my way, if I get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a second trade is something you push away. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not a classroom person, and I left school at sixteen. Last time I sat an exam I froze. But I'd rather learn gas fitting with a real person showing me than sit at a screen, so if it came to it, I'd try.

say: I'd say five years is enough for the government to set up **proper help**.
I'd say don't leave it to companies, who only see the **next quarter**.
think: I could get a few years of **driving** in before robots do hands-on work.
After that I'd be forty and need a **second trade**, which I push away.
do: Get the **HGV licence** this year and take any decent driving job.
Save what I can once in work and look at a **second skill** like gas fitting.
Talk to **Pete and Tony** before any big decision.
feel: A bit steadier, with a short runway, though I'm still at the **back of the queue**.
S3.quote: In 2031 I could get a job, do it for two or three years, and use that time to learn something else.
fieldNote: Treats five years as **time to earn**, then learn a second trade.
His barrier is **classroom fear**, not unwillingness to learn.
Plans with his brother and friend, not alone.

steps.text: Finish the HGV licence and take the first decent driving job
Look into a gas fitting course taught on site with a real tutor
Save a little from each wage once in work
Talk through any big move with Pete and my brother Tony

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'll be forty-four, and that's long enough that I'd think I'd have found a proper place by then. I'd say that's one I could cope with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to sort things out, if the government does something instead of making speeches. I'd tell people not to fret, but to get a trade in their hands. I'd say it at the snooker club, I don't do online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd manage ten years. I'd work and drive, save a bit, get a second trade over time. I'd probably still worry whether it holds, because I can't see the finish line, but I've got more than enough working years to make a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drive for a few years, keep up the licence and forklift tickets, then take an evening course in something like electrical installation. I'd save a little every month and try to buy a small flat with a mortgage, so I've got a roof. I'd also have Lena show me how to use the phone better, step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, but not carefree. Ten years of working isn't nothing, but I'd still have to get a job first, and that's where my stomach tightens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Lena to teach you on the phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Banking, the jobs app and how to book appointments without waiting on hold. If I can do those three, I'd feel I'm not stuck in the nineties. I'd do it on a Sunday afternoon over a cuppa, nice and slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If ten years goes the way you say, what would that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A steady job, a small flat with my name on it and a trade in reserve. That's all I want, honestly, nothing fancy. A quiet life where the van starts in the morning and the work's there.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty if the government does something **instead of speeches**.
I'd tell people to get a **trade** in their hands.
think: I'd manage ten years: **work, save** and learn a second trade slowly.
I'd still worry, because I can't see the **finish line**.
do: Drive for a few years, then take an evening course in **electrical installation**.
Save monthly towards a small **flat** with a mortgage.
Have my niece Lena teach me **banking and booking** on the phone.
feel: Mostly calm, but not carefree, since I still need a **job first**.
S4.quote: A steady job, a small flat with my name on it and a trade in reserve. That's all I want, honestly, nothing fancy.
fieldNote: A **modest dream**: job, flat, trade in reserve.
Digital skills he'd learn from **family**, slowly, not on his own.
Anxious even in the longest scenario because the first job is still unsecured.

steps.text: Drive for a few years and keep the licence and forklift ticket current
Take an evening electrical installation course
Save a little every month towards a deposit on a small flat
Ask Lena to teach me banking and booking on the phone

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Two years is too quick for a man with no savings, no clear trade to fall back on, and no great head for apps. What would help is a proper job at the end of any retraining, help in person and not online, and a payment that covers rent while I learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't against progress. We just want somebody to explain it slowly, in person, and not hand us a login. And I'd like some honest word on whether driving's got a future.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't against progress. We just want somebody to explain it slowly, in person, and not hand us a login.
portrait: Karl is **34**, lives alone in Stanmoor, and has been on **benefits only** since Hollis Bakeries closed his depot in June.
He drove a delivery van for six years and wants a **driving job** again, preferably with a small firm.
He avoids AI and struggles with online accounts, but will **follow family** if an app is the only way in.
He blames mergers and chains rather than technology, and his mood is **anxious** in most scenarios and alarmed at two years.
His dream is modest: a steady job, a small flat and a **spare trade**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too fast with no savings and no trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **real job** at the end of any retraining, with help in person.
A payment that covers **rent** while he learns.
